prompt: Consider the view that all thinking is a bodily process like perceiving, as the ancients held, and evaluate whether Aristotle's critique of this view depends on his theory of phantasia.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis The ancient philosophers, Aristotle reports, regard thinking as a bodily process analogous to perceiving, holding that like is known by like and that the soul's cognitive operations are therefore materially constituted in the same manner as sense-reception (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 22–23). Against this thesis Aristotle marshals a sustained critique whose force depends, as we shall see, upon his articulation of phantasia as a faculty irreducible to either perception or thought. The ancients' conflation rests on a failure to distinguish the several modalities through which the soul apprehends its objects; indeed, if perceiving and thinking were identical in kind, one could not account for the pervasive phenomenon of error, since perception of proper sensibles is always true, whereas thought and phantasia admit of falsity (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 3–4). As Caston argues, "for Aristotle's inference to be valid, the thesis must maintain only that thinking consists in the same kind of process as perceiving, not strict identity" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 3–4); accordingly, the critique targets the structural homology the ancients presuppose between perceiving and thinking rather than a naïve claim of material equivalence. Aristotle's account of phantasia is grounded in the prior operation of sense-perception—aisthesis—such that the image-making faculty cannot function independently of sensory contact with particulars, yet it contrasts with aisthesis insofar as phantasia can operate in the absence of the perceived object and, crucially, can be false where perception of proper sensibles cannot (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). The internal differentiation of phantasia into sensory and deliberative grades, as well as its complex relation to doxa, will receive fuller treatment below; here it suffices the very possibility of distinguishing phantasia from aisthesis constitutes Aristotle's primary weapon against the materialist reduction of all cognition to bodily affection. Heidegger, reading the broader context of Aristotle's psychology, emphasises that the πάθη are "not states pertaining to ensouled things, but are concerned with a disposition of living things in their world, in the mode of being positioned toward something" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 96–98), a remark that underscores how the soul's capacities—including phantasia—are not mere bodily processes but ways of being-toward the world. 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia The phantasma—the sensory image produced and retained by the faculty of phantasia—occupies a pivotal and conceptually fraught position in Aristotle's philosophy of mind, for it serves simultaneously as the medium through which the soul contemplates absent objects and as the representational vehicle that links perception to thought. As Aristotle insists, "the soul never thinks without a phantasma" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 25–27); thus every act of intellection, however abstract, depends upon the image-making capacity of phantasia, and the phantasma functions as the indispensable bridge between the bodily reception of sense-data and the exercise of nous. Nussbaum observes that in *De Anima* III.7, Aristotle speaks of calculation about the future "as though it involved a kind of picturing: 'When one calculates, using the phantasmata or noëmata in the soul, as if one saw the things, and plans for the future in view of the present'" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 53–55); the inclusion of noëmata alongside phantasmata signals that the phantasma is not reducible to a literal mental picture but functions as whatever content presents itself to the soul's apprehensive gaze in the absence of the object. Caston emphasises that phantasia can be false, noting that Aristotle "says that a scene-painting or a dream are both 'something, but not what they produce a phantasia of'" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16); hence the phantasma possesses an intentional structure—it is of something other than itself—that distinguishes it from the direct deliverances of aisthesis. 

## 3. Phantasia and Mneme Memory, for Aristotle, is not a simple retrieval of past perceptions but rather presupposes the mediating operation of phantasia, insofar as every act of remembering requires a phantasma that functions at once as an object of present contemplation and as a likeness of the thing remembered. This dual nature of the phantasma—simultaneously θεώρημα and εἰκών—generates what we may call the representational puzzle at the heart of Aristotle's account: how does the soul recognise a present image as a likeness of an absent thing without already possessing access to the absent thing itself? Bowin, commenting on the relationship between memory and time-perception, notes that Aristotle uses a broader sense of "perceive" to emphasise that "memory is a perceptual and not an intellectual activity" (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, pp. 8–10); yet this very broadening reveals how phantasia contrasts with mneme, since phantasia can generate images that are not tethered to a determinate past event, whereas memory is essentially temporal—it concerns what has been. Furthermore, as Bowin reports, Aristotle holds that "animals have no universal beliefs (καθόλου ὑπόληψιν) but only imagination (φαντασία) and memory (μνήμη) of particulars" (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, p. 14); thus animals possess both phantasia and mneme without possessing doxa or intellectual capacity, which confirms that the ancients' conflation of thinking with perceiving cannot account for the stratified cognitive economy Aristotle attributes even to non-rational souls. The bearing on the central question is therefore clear: because Aristotle's critique of the materialist thesis requires him thought involves capacities beyond mere bodily affection, his differentiation of phantasia from memory—and his insistence that both operate beneath the threshold of intellection—provides the intermediate conceptual architecture that the ancients lacked. The distinction between sensory phantasia, which animals share, and deliberative phantasia, available only to rational beings who can combine phantasmata into composite representations, further refines the account and will be considered in its relation to doxa immediately below. 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa If imagination were identical to opinion, Aristotle argues, then either the true opinion disappears inexplicably or it becomes simultaneously true and false—an impossibility that compels us to distinguish phantasia from doxa as genuinely different psychic capacities (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 25–27). [PAGE NEEDED]) phantasia and doxa have different truth-conditions, different relations to voluntariness, and different distributions across the animal kingdom, the materialist reduction fails at every joint. White reports that Aristotle objects that the materialist view—that like is known by like—cannot account for error (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 23); accordingly, the phenomenon of false phantasia without false doxa becomes the decisive counterexample. O'Gorman, situating phantasia within the rhetorical tradition, notes that Aristotle treats "bringing before the eyes" as a lexical form of energeia, a type of motion realised through the mind's capacity for seeing objects in action (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 5); this rhetorical dimension confirms that phantasia operates as an active presentation—something one does, voluntarily, in deliberative contexts—rather than a passive bodily reception. Thus Aristotle's critique of the ancients depends essentially upon his theory of phantasia: without the conceptual distinction between aisthesis, phantasma, mneme, and doxa that phantasia both mediates and makes visible, the materialist thesis would remain unchallenged, and the soul's cognitive life would collapse into the undifferentiated bodily process the pre-Socratics envisaged.
